notes.heading: Rate as concentration change per time
points: Average rate v = |Δc| / Δt. Never negative, so use the absolute value. Usual units: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
Species with different mole ratios change at different rates. Divide each rate by its coefficient to get the overall rate.
Instantaneous rate is the gradient of a tangent to a concentration–time curve at that moment.
Initial rate is the tangent gradient at t = 0. Divide by the coefficient for overall rate.
Mass, volume, pressure, pH, conductivity or colour can track rate. Rate is then in units of that quantity per second.

notes.heading: Collisions need energy and orientation
points: Reaction needs particles to collide, with correct mutual orientation and enough total kinetic energy.
Most collisions are unsuccessful: the particles bounce apart without chemical change.
Wrong orientation fails even when energy is high enough.
Symmetrical particles such as atoms and monatomic ions react regardless of orientation, so they tend to react faster.

notes.heading: Factors that change reaction rate
points: Higher concentration or gas pressure means more frequent collisions, so a faster rate. Pressure does not affect reactions with no gaseous reactants.
Larger surface area (smaller solid pieces) gives more frequent collisions at the surface, so a faster rate.
These three factors change collision frequency only. The proportion of successful collisions stays the same.
Higher temperature gives more frequent collisions and a larger fraction with Ek ≥ Ea. Rate often rises two to four times per 10°C.
Maxwell–Boltzmann curve at higher T: flatter, broader, peak moves right, more particles above Ea.

notes.heading: Activation energy
points: Ea is the minimum kinetic energy colliding particles need for a successful collision.
If total Ek < Ea, the collision always fails. If Ek ≥ Ea, it succeeds only with correct orientation.
On an energy profile, Ea is the gap from reactants up to the transition state, the highest-energy, least stable arrangement.
Exothermic: products lower than reactants (ΔH < 0). Endothermic: products higher (ΔH > 0).

notes.heading: Catalysts lower activation energy
points: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not consumed. It gives an alternative pathway with lower Ea.
More particles then have energy ≥ Ea, so a greater proportion of collisions succeed.
A catalyst does not change ΔH or the average kinetic energy. Temperature changes average Ek but not Ea.
Catalysed pathway usually has several steps, with an intermediate that can exist for a time. A transition state cannot.
Enzymes are biological catalysts (proteins). Each is very specific to one or a few reactions.

notes.heading: Multistep reactions and rate-determining step
points: A mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps. The slowest step, the rate-determining step (RDS), limits the overall rate.
The RDS usually has the highest Ea. It need not be the first step.
Intermediates are formed in one step and used in a later one, so they are absent from the overall equation.
A proposed mechanism must not contradict experimental rate data. Steps must add up to the overall equation.
Example: if CO concentration does not affect rate, CO enters after the RDS.

notes.heading: Energy profiles for multistep reactions
points: Number of transition states = number of steps. Number of intermediates = steps minus one.
Less stable species sit higher. An intermediate is less stable than both reactants and products.
The RDS usually has the highest Ea peak.
Label axes energy and reaction coordinate. Label reactants, products, intermediates, transition states and Ea.

notes.heading: Molecularity of elementary steps
points: Molecularity is the number of species reacting in one elementary step.
Unimolecular: one species. Bimolecular: two colliding species. Termolecular: three, which is very rare.
Termolecular steps are rare because three particles seldom collide together in the correct orientation.

notes.heading: Rate equations come from experiment
points: Rate equation form: rate = k[A]^n[B]^m. Products do not appear.
Orders cannot be read from the balanced equation's coefficients. They depend on mechanism.
Orders are found experimentally by changing concentrations and measuring initial rate.
A known mechanism and RDS can give the rate equation, and a measured rate equation can test a mechanism.

notes.heading: Reaction order and graphs
points: Order is the exponent of a concentration in the rate equation. Overall order is the sum of the exponents.
Doubling [A]: rate doubles means first order. Rate ×4 means second order. No change means zero order.
Rate–concentration graphs: zero order horizontal line; first order straight line through origin; second order parabola.
Concentration–time: zero order is a straight line with slope −k. First and second order curves look alike, so plot ln[A] or 1/[A] against t.
Straight ln[A] vs t means first order (slope −k). Straight 1/[A] vs t means second order (slope +k).

notes.heading: Rate constant and its units
points: k is specific to a reaction and depends on temperature, so keep T constant when comparing runs.
Find k by substituting concentrations and initial rate into the rate equation, then rearranging.
Units come from the overall order: zero mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, first s⁻¹, second dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹, third dm⁶ mol⁻² s⁻¹.
Work out units by putting units into rate = k[...] and solving for k.

notes.heading: Arrhenius equation and activation energy
points: k = A e^(−Ea/RT). The linear form is ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A. Both forms are in the data booklet.
Plot ln k against 1/T: a straight line with gradient −Ea/R and y-intercept ln A.
Two-point form: ln(k1/k2) = (Ea/R)(1/T2 − 1/T1). At constant concentrations, rate ratio equals k ratio.
Convert Ea to kJ mol⁻¹ and T to kelvin. Gradient is in K.

notes.heading: The Arrhenius factor A
points: A covers the frequency of collisions with proper orientation. It is specific to each reaction and nearly independent of T.
Simple, symmetrical particles give high A. Large molecules needing specific orientation give low A.
A has the same units as k. Find them from the rate equation.
Find A from the intercept (ln A) of the Arrhenius plot, or by substituting a point on the line.

definitions.definition: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
definitions.trap: Saying 'time taken for reaction to finish' or leaving out concentration.

definitions.definition: The rate at one particular moment, found as the gradient of the tangent to a concentration–time curve at that time.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with the average rate over a time interval.

definitions.definition: The instantaneous rate of reaction at time zero, found from the tangent gradient at t = 0.
definitions.trap: Forgetting to divide by the stoichiometric coefficient for the overall rate.

definitions.definition: The minimum energy colliding particles must have for a successful collision that leads to reaction.
definitions.trap: Omitting the word 'minimum', which examiners repeatedly flag as losing the mark.

definitions.definition: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, without being consumed.
definitions.trap: Saying a catalyst changes ΔH or raises the average kinetic energy.

definitions.definition: The least stable, highest-energy arrangement of atoms along the reaction pathway, in which bonds are partly broken and partly formed.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with an intermediate, which can exist for a time.

definitions.definition: An unstable species formed in one step and consumed in a later step, able to exist for a time in the mixture.
definitions.trap: Mixing it up with a transition state, or listing it as a reactant or product.

definitions.definition: The sequence of elementary steps by which reactants are converted into products.
definitions.trap: Treating a mechanism as proven rather than a hypothesis consistent with data.

definitions.definition: A single step in which one, two or three species change through one transition state with no intermediates.
The slowest elementary step in a mechanism, which limits the overall rate of reaction.
definitions.trap: Assuming it is always the first step.

definitions.definition: The number of reacting particles taking part in an elementary step.
definitions.trap: Confusing molecularity with reaction order, which is found from experiment.

definitions.definition: The exponent to which the concentration of a reactant is raised in the rate equation.
definitions.trap: Taking the order from the balanced equation's coefficient, or ignoring the power of concentration.

definitions.definition: The sum of the orders with respect to each reactant in the rate equation.
The proportionality constant k in the rate equation, specific to a reaction and dependent on temperature; units depend on overall order.
definitions.trap: Giving k the wrong units, or saying it depends on concentration.

definitions.definition: The factor A in the Arrhenius equation, which accounts for the frequency of collisions with proper orientation.
definitions.trap: Forgetting that A has the same units as k.
